title: "Chapter 3 · History & Culture"

{{< include ../../_includes/lang-switcher/module-03.en.qmd >}}

If Chapters 1 and 2 were a close-up of the leaf and the body, this chapter steps back. The wider view is **who moved the leaf**, and **how people staged the cup**.

Along the way, tea remade **trade balances** between China and Britain. It became a **monastic focus aid** and a tea-room practice. After the monopoly break, **plantations** remade land and labor into a cheap mass commodity. Living **regional scripts**—Chaoshan tables, Hong Kong milk-tea counters, Taiwan tea art—still stage the drink as culture.

Warmth priming and ritual-stress psychology used to share this chapter. They now live next door, in [Chapter 4 · Context & Ritual Psychology](../module-04/index.qmd). History stays narrative here.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Words to know on this journey (open if you want labels)"}
- **Canton System** — the Qing rule (1757–1842) that funneled Western trade through Canton and demanded payment in silver.
- **Opium Wars** — the conflicts (1839–1860) that forced trade openings after the silver–tea–opium crisis.
- **Chado** — Japan's highly ritualized "way of tea."
- **Gongfu tea (Chaoshan)** — everyday staging with a small pot and repeated cups, a culture script rather than a lab ritual.
- **Plantation aftershock** — the land, the labor, and the commodity form that followed once Chinese monopoly leaf ceased to be the only farm.
:::

**Read the story; open More detail boxes only when curious.** History and culture stay on the open path, and the denser tables live behind the click.
